text: The Golden Temple, also known as Harimandir Sahib or Durbār Sahib, is a gurdwara located in Amritsar, Punjab, India, and is the pre-eminent spiritual site of Sikhism, alongside the Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur and the Gurdwara Janam Asthan in Nankana Sahib, both in Punjab, Pakistan. The sarovar (holy pool) on the site was completed by the fourth Sikh Guru, Guru Ram Das, in 1577. In 1604, Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh Guru, placed a copy of the Adi Granth in the Golden Temple and played a key role in its development. The gurdwara was repeatedly rebuilt by the Sikhs after facing persecution and was destroyed several times by the Mughal and invading Afghan armies. Maharaja Ranjit Singh, after founding the Sikh Empire, rebuilt it in marble and copper in 1809 and overlaid the sanctum with gold leaf in 1830, leading to its name "Golden Temple." The Golden Temple is spiritually the most significant shrine in Sikhism and became a center of the Singh Sabha Movement (1883–1920s) and the Punjabi Suba Movement (1947–1966). In the early 1980s, it became a center of conflict between the Indian government and a radical movement led by Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale. In 1984, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi ordered Operation Blue Star, a military action from 1 to 8 June 1984, to remove Bhindranwale and his followers from the complex, resulting in thousands of deaths among soldiers, militants, and civilians, significant damage to the gurdwara, and the destruction of the nearby Akal Takht—the prime seat of Sikh authority. The gurdwara complex was subsequently rebuilt. The Golden Temple is an open house of worship for all people, with a square plan, four entrances, and a circumambulation path around the pool; the four entrances symbolize Sikh beliefs in equality and inclusivity. The complex includes the Akal Takht, a clock tower, offices of the Gurdwara Committee, a museum, and a langar—a free vegetarian kitchen serving all visitors without discrimination. Over 150,000 people visit daily. The site has been nominated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with its application pending on the tentative list. The land for the site was chosen by Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, and named Guru Da Chakk; Guru Ram Das founded the town Ramdaspur, which later became Amritsar, after acquiring the land—either through donations of 700 rupees from the village of Tung or a donation from Emperor Akbar to Ram Das’s wife. Construction began in 1581, with the pool kept dry for eight years; Guru Arjan designed the gurdwara at a lower level to emphasize humility and ensured the compound was open on all sides to promote inclusivity. The sanctum had only one bridge, symbolizing the unity of the end goal. In 1589, the brick gurdwara was completed; some sources claim Guru Arjan invited the Sufi saint Mian Mir to lay the foundation stone, though this is unsubstantiated; traditional sources state he laid it himself. After the inauguration, the pool was filled with water, and on 16 August 1604, Guru Arjan completed the Adi Granth and appointed Baba Buddha as the first Granthi. The Ath Sath Tirath, a raised canopy on the circumambulation path, reflects the belief that visiting the temple is equivalent to 68 Hindu pilgrimage sites. The completion of the first version of the Golden Temple was a major milestone, providing a central pilgrimage site. Guru Arjan’s growing influence drew Mughal attention; he was arrested by Emperor Jahangir, tortured, and executed in 1606. His son, Guru Hargobind, fought a battle at Amritsar and left in 1635 for Kiratpur. The temple was occupied by the Minas for about a century. In the 18th century, Guru Gobind Singh sent Bhai Mani Singh to reclaim it. The temple remained a target of persecution by Mughal rulers and Afghan Sultans. After destruction, it was reconstructed in 1764 (confirmed by H.H. Cole) or 1776 (per Giani Gian Singh’s Tawarikh Sri Amritsar), with most decorations added in the early 19th century. Ranjit Singh, at age 22 in 1802, took Amritsar from the Bhangi Misl, paid homage at the temple, and announced plans to rebuild it in marble and gold. He donated gilded copper panels worth 500,000 rupees, with Mistri Yar Muhammad Khan overseeing the work under Bhai Sand Singh; the first panel was placed in 1803. Various individuals, including Tara Singh Gheba, Partap Singh, Jodh Singh, and Ganda Singh Peshawari (who donated in 1823), contributed to the ceiling decoration. Raja Sangat Singh of Jind State helped with the Darshani Deori. Due to the temple’s central importance, every Sikh sardar contributed to its renovations. The temple was renovated in marble and copper in 1809 and gold-leafed in 1830; an inscription at the entrance commemorates the work by Ranjit Singh and Giani Sant Singh of the Giani Samparda. A Gurmukhi inscription states that Maharaja Ranjit Singh was regarded as the chief servitor of the Great Guru. The 7th Nizam of Hyderabad, Mir Osman Ali Khan, began annual grants after learning of the temple through Ranjit Singh. Ranjit Singh took over management of the Durbar Sahib complex, appointing Sardar Desa Singh Majithia and making land grants to fund operations. Hari Singh Nalwa decorated the Akal Takht with gold and added the golden dome. Ranjit Singh made the position of temple officials hereditary; the Giani family were the only ones allowed to perform Katha from 1788 until 1921, when the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee took over, and they built the Bungas around the temple, including the gold and marble overlay. One of the main Bungas destroyed in 1988 was the Burj Gianian; the Kapurs were made heads of the Granthis, including ancestors of Bhai Jawahir Singh Kapur, who attempted but was denied the position. The temple complex was destroyed during Operation Blue Star, a military operation from 1 to 8 June 1984, ordered by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi after Harchand Singh Longowal invited Bhindranwale to reside in the complex to evade arrest. The government claimed Bhindranwale turned the temple into an armory and headquarters. After failed negotiations, the army attacked on 3 June 1984, with fighting lasting three days and ending on 8 June. The army used tanks and heavy artillery, facing resistance from militants with rocket-propelled grenade launchers and fortified positions at the Akal Takht. Casualty figures include 83 dead and 249 injured among soldiers, 1,592 militants apprehended, and 493 militant and civilian casualties; the government attributed high civilian deaths to militants using pilgrims as human shields. Foreign reporter Brahma Chellaney, the only one to remain in Amritsar, reported a death toll about twice the official figure—780 militants and civilians and 400 troops—stating that eight to ten men suspected of being militants were shot with hands tied and that a doctor was forced to perform postmortems. The Indian government charged Chellaney with violating press censorship, fanning sectarian hatred, and sedition. The operation was widely criticized by Sikhs worldwide as an assault on their religion, leading to many Sikh soldiers deserting and civil servants resigning. Five months later, on 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards, Satwant Singh and Beant Singh. The public outcry led to over 3,000 Sikh killings in Delhi during the 1984 anti-Sikh riots. Following the operation, hundreds of houses were demolished, and a security corridor called Galliara (Galiara or Galyara) was created around the compound and later opened as a public park in June 1988.

The military action in the temple complex was criticized by Sikhs worldwide, who viewed it as an assault on the Sikh religion. Many Sikh soldiers deserted their units, and several Sikhs resigned from civil administrative offices, returning awards received from the Indian government. Five months after the operation, on 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her two Sikh bodyguards, Satwant Singh and Beant Singh, in an act of revenge. Public outrage over her death led to the killing of more than 3,000 Sikhs in Delhi during the 1984 anti-Sikh riots. Following the operation, the central government demolished hundreds of houses and created a security corridor called "Galliara" (also spelled Galiara or Galyara) around the compound. This corridor was later transformed into a public park and opened in June 1988. In December 2021, a young man was allegedly beaten to death after disrupting the Rehras Sahib (evening prayer) at the sanctum by jumping over a railing, picking up the sword before the Guru Granth Sahib, and attempting to touch it; he was overpowered by pilgrims and suffered fatal head injuries. The 2023 Golden Temple blasts occurred on 7 May and 9 May 2023. The Golden Temple's architecture reflects various architectural practices from the Indian subcontinent, with the first Harmandir Sahib built by Guru Arjan combining dharamsaals and holy water tanks (sarovar), constructed lower than the surroundings so devotees would have to walk down to reach it. The four entrances symbolize openness to all four traditional Indian caste classifications (varnas). No surviving record of the pre-1764 Harmandir Sahib built by the Sikh gurus exists, though Kanwarjit Singh Kang believes the original structure was similar to the 1764 version. James Fergusson considered the temple a specimen of 19th-century Hindu temple architecture. The colonial Punjab government in 1875 claimed the design, as built by Ranjit Singh, was based on the shrine of Sufi saint Mian Mir. Louis Rousselet described it as a "handsome style of Jat architecture," while Major Henry Hardy Cole noted it drew primarily from Islamic sources with Hindu influences. Percy Brown classified it as a synthesis of Islamic and Hindu styles with unique characteristics. Hermann Goetz viewed it as a "Kangra transformation of Oudh architecture," praising it but criticizing its "gaudy" elements, such as rococo-style art. Scholars like Ian Kerr describe it as a mixture of Indo-Islamic Mughal and Hindu Rajput architecture. The sanctum is 12.25 x 12.25 metres with two storeys and a gold leaf dome, sitting on a 19.7 x 19.7 metre marble platform within a 154.5 x 148.5 m² pool called Amritsar or Amritsarovar, which is 5.1 metres deep and surrounded by a 3.7-metre-wide circumambulatory marble passage. The sanctum is connected to the platform by a causeway, with the gateway called the Darshani Deorhi. Pilgrims can take a dip in the pool, believed to purify karma, and some carry water home for sick relatives. The pool is maintained by volunteers through periodic kar seva, including draining and desilting. The Har-Ki-Pauri section, located on the back of the temple, provides water for sipping and daily cleaning, with the cleaning solution mixed with milk. The Guru Granth Sahib is seated on the lower floor for about 20 hours daily and moved to its bedroom in the Akal Takht for four hours each day for sukhasana and Prakash. The upper floor is a gallery connected by stairs. The ground floor and surrounding path are lined with white marble, the exterior has gilded copper plates, doors are gold leaf-covered copper with nature motifs, the upper ceiling is gilded, embossed, and decorated with jewels, and the dome is semi-spherical with a pinnacle. The sides have arched copings and small domes, with corners adorned by cupolas, all covered in gold leaf. A pavilion called the Shish Mahal (mirror room) is on the second floor. Floral designs on the walls are Arabesque, arches contain verses from the Guru Granth Sahib in gold letters, and frescoes include animal, bird, and nature motifs. Stair walls feature murals of Sikh Gurus, such as a falcon carrying Guru Gobind Singh on horseback. The Darshani Deorhi houses temple management offices and treasury. The Prasada facility serves Karah prasad, a flour-based sweet offering. Pilgrims enter and circumambulate clockwise around the pool before entering the sanctum. There are four entrances to the gurdwara complex, symbolizing openness, but only one entrance to the sanctum via a causeway. In front of the sanctum is the Akal Takht, the chief Takht meaning "throne of the Timeless (God)," established by Guru Hargobind after his father's martyrdom as a center for spiritual and secular affairs, issuing binding writs. The Akal Takht is also known as Takht Sri Akal Bunga and is the primary seat among the five Sikh Takhts, located in Anandpur, Patna, Nanded, Talwandi Sabo, and Amritsar. It is the headquarters of the Shiromani Akali Dal (Supreme Akali Party). The Teja Singh Samundri Hall is the office of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, overseeing major Sikh temples. The Ramgarhia Bunga, two red sandstone minaret-style towers visible from the parikrama, was built in the 18th century by Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, a Sikh warrior and Ramgarhia misl chief, as watchtowers to defend against military raids. Over 70 such Bungas were built during the 18th century to house soldiers, provide accommodation, and serve as centers of learning; most were demolished during British rule, but the Ramgarhia Bunga remains a symbol of the community's identity and historical defense. The Clock Tower did not exist originally; in its place was a building called the "lost palace," which the British wanted to demolish after the Second Anglo-Sikh War. The Sikhs opposed it, but the demolition proceeded. The clock tower, designed by John Gordon in a Gothic style with red bricks, was built from 1862 to 1874 and later demolished by the Sikh community about 70 years later. A new entrance on the north side was constructed in its place, featuring a clock, a museum on the upper floor, and continuing to be called ghanta ghar deori. The original complex was open with many trees; now it is a walled, two-storey courtyard with four entrances, preserving three Ber trees. One, to the right of the main ghanta ghar deori, is called Ber Baba Buddha, believed to be where Baba Buddha sat during the pool and temple construction. A second, Laachi Ber, is where Guru Arjan rested during construction. The third, Dukh Bhanjani Ber, is on the other side of the sanctum, where a Sikh was cured of leprosy after bathing, earning it the name "suffering remover"; a small gurdwara is beneath it. The Ath Sath Tirath, or equivalent of 68 pilgrimages, is under this tree, and bathing nearby is believed to offer the same spiritual benefits as visiting 68 pilgrimage sites. The main north entrance has a Sikh history museum on the first floor, displaying paintings of gurus and martyrs, and historical items like swords, kartar, comb, and chakkars. A new underground museum near the clock tower also shows Sikh history. According to Louis E. Fenech, the display emphasizes persecution, martyrdom, and bravery, though it is partly ahistorical, such as a headless body continuing to fight. The main entrance has memorial plaques commemorating Sikh historical events, saints, martyrs, Ranjit Singh's contributions, and all Sikh soldiers who died in the two World Wars and Indo-Pakistan wars. The Amrit Sarovar is the main temple tank, measuring approximately 150 meters by 150 meters, with the shrine in the center, surrounded by a marble walkway. Construction began in November 1573 under Guru Amar Das, with major work by Guru Ram Das and expansion by Guru Arjan. The Udasis of Brahm Buta Akhara dug a hansli in 1783 to feed the sarovar, later made redundant by the construction of the Amritsar-Lahore and Kasur-Sabraon branches. Since 1866, the sarovar has been fed from the Jethuwal distributory of the Upper Bari Doab between the Beas and Ravi, via a connection between Kaulsar Sarovar and Amrit Sarovar; the canal was originally kachcha but later lined and covered. Since the 1900s, the sarovar has been regularly cleaned through kar seva, with the first modern cleaning held on 17 June 1923. Other prominent sarovars in Amritsar include Santokhsar, Ramsar, Kaulsar, and Bibeksar. Daily rites treat the Guru Granth Sahib as a living person, including ceremonies for its seating and movement. The complex includes a langar, a community-run free kitchen and dining hall attached to the east side near the Dukh Bhanjani Ber, outside the entrance. Vegetarian food is served to all visitors regardless of faith, gender, or economic status, with everyone sitting on the floor in rows called sangat. Over 100,000 meals are served daily. The art of the Golden Temple has rarely been seriously studied. The Shish Mahal features mirror-work with small mirror pieces inlaid into walls and ceilings, highlighted by floral designs. Ceilings, walls, and arches are embellished with intricate murals. Pietra dura artwork, featuring avian and animal designs using semi-precious stones, is inspired by Mughal tradition. The premises are also decorated with embossed copper, gach, tukri, jaratkari, and ivory inlay. External upper walls have beaten copper plates with raised floral and abstract designs, including human figures. Two embossed copper panels on the front depict Guru Nanak with companions Bhai Mardana and Bhai Bala, and an equestrian portrayal of Guru Gobind Singh. Gach is a type of stone or gypsum, transformed into paste and applied to walls like lime-plaster, then decorated with steel cutters and tools; colored glass pieces placed on it are known as tukri, with many examples in the Shish Mahal. Jaratkari involves placing inlaid and cut stones of various colors and types into marble, with surviving examples found in the temple.

Plates at the Golden Temple often feature raised designs, typically floral or abstract, though some include human figures. Two embossed copper panels on the front of the temple prior depict Guru Nanak with his companions, Bhai Mardana and Bhai Bala, on either side, and another shows an equestrian portrayal of Guru Gobind Singh. Gach, a type of stone or gypsum, was transformed into a paste similar to lime-plaster and applied to walls, where it was shaped using steel cutters and other tools; sometimes coloured glass pieces, known as tukri, were embedded, as seen extensively in the Shish Mahal. Jaratkari, an art form involving inlaid and cut stones of various colours and types into marble, is found on the lower exterior walls of the temple, using semi-precious stones like lapis lazuli and onyx, classified as pietra dura. Unlike Mughal jaratkari, which does not include human or animal figuratives, Sikh jaratkari art features such depictions. Inlaid ivory work is visible on the doors of the Darshani Deori, constructed from shisham wood, with the front overlaid in silverwork and the back adorned with floral, geometric, and animal designs including deer, tigers, lions, and birds; portions of the ivory were coloured red or green, praised by H.H. Cole for their harmony. The oldest surviving murals date to the 1830s, with most destroyed during renovations under the guise of kar seva, such as by covering walls with marble slabs. A prominent mural artist was Gian Singh Naqqash, whose works include floral designs with scattered animal themes and over 300 distinct patterns across the walls. Naqqashi artists developed a specialized language for their designs, with the most prominent category being dehin, defined as an imaginative expression of idealised forms, rooted in gharwanjh—a decorative motif of knotted animals like cobras, lions, and elephants holding or carrying floral vases with fruit and fairies—while the border of dehin is called patta, often featuring creepers or aquatic creatures. The only mural of human figures inside the temple is on the wall behind the northern staircase, depicting Guru Gobind Singh on horseback with his retinue leaving Anandpur, adapted from a Kangra miniature painting. H.H. Cole noted that murals of Indic mythological scenes once existed but have since been lost. W. Wakefield reported erotic murals in 1875, but Kanwarjit Singh Kang considers this account spurious due to lack of corroboration. Most artists and craftsmen involved in the temple’s artwork remain unidentified, though Hari Singh compiled a list including Kishan Singh, Bishan Singh, Kapur Singh, Kehar Singh, Mahant Ishar Singh, Sardul Singh, Jawahar Singh, Mehtab Singh, Mistri Jaimal Singh, Harnam Singh, Ishar Singh (distinct from Mahant Ishar Singh), Gian Singh, Lal Singh Tarn Taran, Mangal Singh, Mistri Narain Singh, Mistri Jit Singh, Atma Singh, Darja Mal, and Vir Singh. Most lost artwork, especially murals, disappeared over time, beginning in the late 19th century when devotees started donating inlaid marble panels that covered previously painted walls, hiding or destroying the murals. The traditional bungas surrounding the temple, which housed many murals, were demolished over time under the guise of modernisation and expansion of the parikrama, leading to the loss of their artwork. When the Darshani Deori was covered with marble panels, murals by Mahant Ishar Singh were also lost. The Singh Sabha movement, beginning in the 1870s, aimed to reform Sikhism in response to conversions to Christianity and Hinduism, with the Tat Khalsa group becoming dominant by the early 1880s. Before 1905, the Golden Temple had Brahmin priests and idols for over a century, but by the 1890s, reformist Sikhs opposed these practices, and in 1905, under the Tat Khalsa campaign, idols and images were removed. The movement led to the reassertion of the Khalsa in gurdwara administration, displacing the mahant class. In 1919, during the Baisakhi festival, Sikhs gathered at the Golden Temple and proceeded to Jallianwala Bagh, where Colonel Dyer opened fire on a crowd, killing 379 and wounding thousands. This massacre intensified opposition to British rule and led to non-violent protests that pressured the British to transfer control of the Golden Temple’s management and finances to the elected Shiromani Gurudwara Prabandhak Committee (SGPC), which continues to manage it. The Punjabi Suba movement, initiated by the Shiromani Akali Dal in April 1948, demanded a Punjabi-speaking state in East Punjab after the States Reorganisation Commission failed to address linguistic boundaries. The Golden Temple complex served as its main centre, hosting key events such as the 1955 government raid and the Amritsar Convention, where Sikh sentiments were conveyed to the central government. The complex was also a site for speeches, demonstrations, mass arrests, and hunger strikes, with movement leaders residing in huts during such periods. The movement culminated in 1966 with the establishment of the modern state of Punjab and the official recognition of Punjabi in the Gurmukhi script. In the early 1980s, militant groups such as the Dharam Yudh Morcha led by Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, Babbar Khalsa, AISSF, and the National Council of Khalistan occupied the Golden Temple and Akal Takht. In December 1983, Harchand Singh Longowal invited Bhindranwale to reside there, and under General Shabeg Singh’s military leadership, bunkers and observation posts were built, and armed militants were organised at Harmandir Sahib in June 1984. The temple became a site for weapons training, and Shabeg Singh’s defences made a commando operation on foot impossible. Supporters circulated maps proposing historical and future boundaries of Khalsa Sikh territories in northwest India, north Pakistan, and eastern Afghanistan. In June 1984, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi ordered Operation Blue Star, resulting in severe damage, destruction of the Akal Takht, and official death tolls of 492 civilians and 83 Indian soldiers. Within days, around 2,000 Sikh soldiers mutinied and attempted to reach Amritsar to liberate the temple. On 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards. In 1986, her son Rajiv Gandhi ordered repairs to the Akal Takht, which were later removed and rebuilt by Sikhs in 1999.
